analysis.one_liner: Diverts unused mine reclamation funds into the retired coal miners' pension fund.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill was referred to committee and never received a vote before Congress ended; a companion version later passed the House but died in the Senate. Hmm — I should not claim things not in sources. Sources show only introduction and referral. Keep headline: 'The bill sat in committee and never got a vote before the 115th Congress ended.'
analysis.plain_summary: Every year a fixed pot of money from coal fees — up to $490 million — is supposed to be spent on mine cleanups and retired miners' health plans. This bill says any money left over goes into the pension fund for retired coal miners, which is running out of money and could otherwise be cut or taken over by the federal pension insurer. The bill pays for itself by extending federal customs fees for a few months. The pension fund would also face new oversight and would be barred from raising benefits while receiving federal money. The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in committee when Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: About 87,000 retired coal miners and widows drawing from the 1974 United Mine Workers pension fund, whose benefits are at risk because coal companies left the fund without enough contributing employers. Retirees keep their full pension checks. The fund also gets new reporting requirements to Treasury and Congress so lawmakers can see exactly how the money is used.

how_it_helps.text: Sends any of the $490 million in annual abandoned-mine funds not already spoken for into the miners' pension fund each year, until the fund is fully funded.
Prevents a collapse that would push the pension fund onto the federal pension insurer and trigger across-the-board benefit cuts for retirees.
Requires the pension fund to file detailed annual reports on its finances, employers, and benefit changes with Treasury and the pension insurer.

analysis.who_pays: Customs payers — mainly importers, whose merchandise processing fees are extended through May 2026 rather than January 2026. General taxpayers are largely shielded because the offset covers the transfers.

drawbacks.text: Uses federal coal-reclamation money for pensions instead of cleaning up abandoned mines, leaving some reclamation work undone.
Locks contributing coal companies into their existing contribution rates and shields transfers from withdrawal liability, easing the cost pressure on the companies that created the shortfall.
Extends customs user fees, which are effectively passed to consumers through import prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Keeps promises to retirees whose employers left them stranded, at modest cost to importers and abandoned-mine cleanup. The bill includes real guardrails — no benefit increases, strict reporting, and a cutoff when the fund recovers — so it is not a blank check.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on May 11, 2017; the committee never acted and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Introduced with 21 cosponsors from both parties, including senators from major coal states.
Referred to the Senate HELP Committee on the day of introduction and never advanced further in that Congress.
The unrelated Senate pension fix failed as well; the miners' relief only became law in December 2019 via the larger USMCA deal.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retired miners stayed exposed to pension cuts while Congress remained stalled; coal companies that exited the fund faced no federal action forcing them to cover their share. Abandoned-mine cleanup funding stayed available for mine reclamation rather than pensions.

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to send surplus mine-reclamation money to the retired miners' pension fund.

for.name: 21 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, 17 Democrats, 3 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Lamar Alexander
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a markup or vote on it before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — 17 Democrats, 3 Republicans (including Sen. Capito and Sen. Portman), and 1 Independent backed the bill.

industries.industry: Retired coal miners and the United Mine Workers union
industries.note: Retirees would have gotten secure pension payments; the broader public shares an interest in workers not losing retirement benefits they earned.

industries.industry: Coal companies still contributing to the 1974 pension plan
industries.note: The bill required them to keep paying at current rates but also excused federal transfers from counting toward withdrawal liability, softening their exposure if they exit.
Leftover annual reclamation money would have been redirected to pensions instead of mine cleanup.
Customs user fees extended about four months longer to offset the pension spending, a cost ultimately passed to consumers.
